label: Facing a Terminal Diagnosis
framing: To be told your time is short is to have the thing we all push away brought suddenly near, and the fear, the grief, and the disbelief that follow are not a failure of faith but the honest weight of a human being facing the end. Scripture does not pretend death is small, but it stands at the grave and calls death the last enemy, already defeated by a Savior who walked through it ahead of you.
cultural: Our culture hides death, tucking the dying away and refusing to speak the word, so that many face the end with no language for it and no community trained to sit beside them. The Bible numbers our days on purpose, teaching us to count them so we gain a heart of wisdom, and treats a death faced in hope not as defeat but as the door home.
historical: Hezekiah, around 700 BC, was told to set his house in order for he would die, and he wept and prayed and was heard. The church across the centuries developed whole traditions for dying well, from the medieval ars moriendi to the modern hospice movement begun by Dame Cicely Saunders in the 1960s, who insisted the dying deserve to be free of pain, surrounded by care, and treated as living until the very last.
application: Let your doctors and a hospice team care for your body and ease your pain, for this is mercy, not surrender. Tell your family the things that must be said, set your affairs in order, and let your pastor and church walk these days with you, praying, visiting, carrying communion to your room. Grieve what you are losing, and hold, underneath the grief, the promise that the One who conquered the grave goes before you into it.

verses.text: In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’” Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, saying, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what was good in Your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
verses.where: King Hezekiah falls ill, and Isaiah tells him to set his house in order because he will die. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays and weeps bitterly, and God answers with fifteen more years. The story is not a promise that every such prayer will be answered the same way; it is a witness that a dying person may weep and plead before God, and that God hears.

verses.text: Going a little farther, He fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour would pass from Him. “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”
verses.where: In Gethsemane Jesus falls to the ground again and again and asks the Father to take the cup from him, and in the same prayer gives his will to the Father's. The church has always read this as the prayer of one who was truly human and felt the horror of death as a real man would. Fear of dying is not a lack of faith; the Son of God prayed through it.

verses.text: “Show me, O LORD, my end and the measure of my days. Let me know how fleeting my life is. You, indeed, have made my days as handbreadths, and my lifetime as nothing before You. Truly each man at his best exists as but a breath. Selah
verses.where: A man who has tried to keep silent finally prays: show me my end and the measure of my days, let me know how fleeting my life is. Every human life, he says, is only a breath. Then he asks the question that matters: what am I waiting for? My hope is in you.

verses.text: So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.
verses.where: Psalm 90, headed as a prayer of Moses, admits that a human life, even a long one, passes quickly and is gone. Its prayer is not for more days but for wisdom about the days: teach us to number them, so that we may gain a heart of wisdom. A short time can still be a wise time.

verses.text: My times are in Your hands; deliver me from my enemies and from those who pursue me.
verses.where: A man hunted by enemies and worn by grief says to God: you are my God, my times are in your hands. The psalm that holds this line also holds the words Jesus prayed on the cross, into your hands I commit my spirit. Neither the diagnosis nor the doctors hold the final measure of a believer's days.

verses.text: For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if I go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labor for me. So what shall I choose? I do not know. I am torn between the two. I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.
verses.where: Paul writes from prison not knowing whether he will live or die. To live is Christ and to die is gain, he says, because to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better. But he expects to stay, for the sake of the people who need him. His longing is not for death but for Christ, and he holds it together with love for those he would leave.

verses.text: For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing.
verses.where: Facing his own execution, Paul writes to Timothy that he is already being poured out like a drink offering and the time of his departure has come. He has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith, and he looks to the crown the Lord will give. He writes it from prison, and in the same chapter asks Timothy to bring his cloak and his scrolls.

verses.text: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well. In My Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am.
verses.where: On the night before he died, Jesus tells his frightened disciples not to let their hearts be troubled, because there are many rooms in his Father's house and he goes to prepare a place for them. The site's note is careful: Jesus himself was troubled more than once, so this is not a scolding. It is a reason not to be ruled by fear, and the reason is a person and a promise: I will take you to be with me.

verses.text: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?”
verses.where: Standing near his friend's grave, Jesus tells Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, and that whoever believes in him will live even though he dies. The body's death still comes; the life he gives is not ended by it. Then he asks her, and every reader: do you believe this?

verses.text: The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verses.where: Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have died, the first of a harvest still to come. He names death plainly as an enemy, the last one Christ will destroy. Scripture never asks a dying person to call death a friend.

misread.taken: The promise that the prayer offered in faith will restore the sick is sometimes used to tell a dying person, or their family, that healing would surely come if only they believed enough, so that a death is taken as a failure of faith.
misread.says: James tells the sick to call the elders to pray and to anoint them with oil, and he promises that the Lord will raise them up. Christians read the promise in more than one way, as the site's note sets out: many take it as real help that often comes as healing and is finally fulfilled in the resurrection; others stress that it depends on God's will, as Paul's unhealed thorn shows. None of these readings sets prayer against medical care, and none makes an unhealed believer guilty of too little faith. Paul prayed three times and was not healed, and no one in Scripture blames him.
misread.text: And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.

whole: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone. Tell someone you trust, a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counselor; if you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today; and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. To be told your time is short is to have the thing everyone pushes away brought suddenly near. The fear, the grief and the disbelief that follow are not a failure of faith. There are new questions every week: treatments and their costs, what to tell the children, whether to keep working, what you still want to do, who will care for the people you leave. Some people find that the hardest part is not the dying but the waiting, and the way others stop knowing what to say.

Scripture does not pretend death is small. Paul calls it an enemy, the last one. Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept. Jesus fell to the ground in Gethsemane and asked for the cup to pass from him. These are not stories of people who failed to trust God; they are stories of people who brought their whole fear to him. The Bible also refuses to read an illness as a verdict on the person who has it. When Jesus was asked whether a man's suffering was punishment, he said no, and Paul, who prayed for relief and did not receive it, is never blamed for a lack of faith.

Wisdom in this season looks like the psalmist's prayer: teach us to number our days. Many people find it helps to ask what they want these days to hold, and to say the things that need saying while they can, words of love, of thanks, of forgiveness asked and given. It is wise to bring the practical matters into the open with the people you love and the professionals who can help, so that no one is left guessing. It is right to pray for healing, as James tells the sick to do, and right to receive good medical care; the two are not rivals. And it is right to let the church carry you: to ask the elders to pray, to let people bring meals and sit with you, to be honest with a pastor about your fear.

The Christian hope here is not a vague comfort. It is a man who walked through death ahead of us and came out the other side. Jesus told Martha he is the resurrection and the life, and he promised his frightened friends a place prepared in his Father's house. Paul, waiting for execution, could say that to depart and be with Christ is far better, and still choose to stay as long as he was needed. Your times are in God's hands, not only in the hands of the doctors. Death is still an enemy, and it still costs everything. But for those who belong to Christ it is not the end of the story, and it is not the last word about you.
deep.sit: If your days are fewer than you hoped, what is one thing you most want to say, and to whom?

prayer.lead: The opening of Psalm 31 ends with the words Jesus prayed on the cross. Pray them as your own, and let the last line be a trust you are still learning.
prayer.text: In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge; let me never be put to shame; save me by Your righteousness. Incline Your ear to me; come quickly to my rescue. Be my rock of refuge, the stronghold of my deliverance. For You are my rock and my fortress; lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name. You free me from the net laid out for me, for You are my refuge. Into Your hands I commit my spirit; You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth.

careLines.text: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
Seeking help is not a failure of faith.
